cases.answer: Implicit wait is a global timeout that applies to every findElement call. Explicit wait uses WebDriverWait with a condition, like waiting until a button is clickable, and that's what I'd normally use. Fluent wait is an explicit wait where you also set the polling interval and which exceptions to ignore. I wouldn't mix implicit and explicit waits.
cases.notes: Covers all three plus the mixing guidance. 'When each is appropriate' is implied by 'what I'd normally use'.

cases.answer: Implicit wait is the best choice because it waits for every condition, including clickability, across the whole suite. Explicit waits are basically Thread.sleep with a fixed time. Fluent wait is only for mobile tests. You should combine implicit and explicit waits so the timeouts add up predictably.
cases.notes: Several central false claims, including the bank's named misconception.

cases.answer: Use soft assertions when you want to check several independent things, like all the labels on a form, and see every mismatch in one run. The common mistake is forgetting to call assertAll at the end, so the failures are collected but never thrown and the test passes.
Soft assertions let the test continue after a failure so you can see multiple failures in one run. I'd use them for checking many fields on a page.

cases.answer: Browser is the actual browser instance that gets launched. A context is like a separate incognito profile inside it, with its own cookies and local storage, so tests don't share login state. A page is just a tab in a context, and pages in the same context share cookies.
Browser is the browser. A context is basically the same thing as a page, and each page always gets its own cookies, so two pages are completely isolated from each other.
evidence: basically the same thing as a page

cases.answer: It happens when the element you found earlier is no longer attached to the DOM, for example the page re-rendered or you navigated. The fix is to find it again with its locator after the change, usually after an explicit wait for the new state, instead of keeping the old WebElement around. In page objects I keep locators, not cached elements.

find it again with its locator

cases.answer: StaleElementReferenceException is thrown when the element takes too long to load, so it's basically a timeout. The right recovery is to catch the exception and retry the same WebElement object in a loop until it becomes fresh again.
The DOM node behind the reference got replaced, like after an Ajax refresh. I wait for the refreshed condition and then re-locate by locator rather than reuse the stored element.
evidence: DOM node behind the reference got replaced

cases.answer: I'd use Awaitility, something like await atMost thirty seconds with a poll interval, until the GET returns the expected status, and on timeout it fails and I log the last response I saw. I'd also tag the created record with a unique ID so parallel tests don't pick up each other's data.

cases.answer: During generation the model keeps the attention keys and values for tokens it has already processed, so each new token only computes attention for itself instead of recomputing the whole prefix. It makes decoding faster, but the cache uses memory that grows with sequence length and the number of concurrent requests.
The KV cache stores previous final answers, so if a user asks the same question again the model can return the cached response instantly without generating anything.
